items.title: [ArchDaily] Architecture as Translation: Africanfuturism in Folklore, Film, and Speculative Art
items.content_html: "Take your dream suppressants." The opening line in Wanuri Kahiū's Pumzi, directed at our protagonist Asha, enforces the order of severing ties with hopeful futures and ancestral memories in pasts shared to compel her focus on the perpetual present in the Maitu Community's heterotopia of an enclave. The bird's-eye view shot of the Maitu reveals a sterile, drone-like structure with a panoptic sphere at its center where normal human behavior is medicalized. The layout is built around closed-loop recycling systems as apt as a self-sufficient organism, designed to escape the toxic environment of a sickly Earth, where every pipe and corridor is engineered to harvest human excretion for water generation, thereby absorbing the roles of nature and state both. The community's architecture perfectly translates the film's message with its physicality.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Unearthing the Ground: Architecture and the Politics of Waste
items.content_html: In 1948, Robert Moses established the Fresh Kills Landfill on the western shore of Staten Island. The site, chosen for its remote marshland and cheap land value, was meant to be temporary, but by 1955 it was the largest landfill in the world, receiving up to 29,000 tons of refuse per day at its 1991 peak. By 2001, after more than fifty years of continuous operation, Fresh Kills covered 2,200 acres, roughly three times the area of Central Park, and was, unspectacularly, visible from space. When it started, Moses didn't expect to design a dump but, without calling it that, a new landform with four artificial hills rising up to sixty meters above sea level built entirely from the accumulated residue of eight million daily lives.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The Future as Propaganda: Soviet Architecture in Kazakhstan and the Imagery of a New Era
items.content_html: Practically every history book records 1961 as the year man first reached space, an achievement that placed the Soviet Union at the center of the space race. What not everyone knows is that Yuri Gagarin's journey began in a seemingly unlikely place, more precisely in Kazakhstan. From the Baikonur Cosmodrome, Gagarin set off beyond Earth, inaugurating not only a new era of space exploration but also a history of technology and ambition that would transform this landscape.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Yaesu Daibiru Office Building / Nikken Sekkei
items.content_html: Project Background and Inheritance of Design Thinking - This project is the redevelopment of a tenant office building facing Yaesu-dori Ave., a landmark street in front of Tokyo Station. The former building, designed by leading 20th-century Japanese architect Togo Murano (1891–1984), long defined the character of the streetscape through its distinctive facade combining stone and cast aluminum components. At a time when curtain walls with an aluminum glazing system were becoming widespread, its pursuit of material richness, precision in facade composition, and responsiveness to the street suggested an architectural approach not solely dependent on style.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Casa Vereda / L'Aura Ortín Architecture for Happiness
items.content_html: Casa Vereda stems from a simple idea: to inhabit nature without competing with it. The project blends into the landscape through an architecture that seeks to become part of its surroundings. Volumes, materials, and textures engage in a dialogue with vegetation, light, and the memory of the place, creating a house that seems to have always been there.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Monte Alvo House / NOZ Arquitectura
items.content_html: The architectural tradition of the Alentejo is defined by simplicity of form, functional spaces, and a deep connection with climate and landscape. At the top of Monte Alvo, the house is single-story, positioned to make full use of solar orientation and ensure thermal comfort throughout the year.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Levanger Creative Building / Incube Architecture + Praksis Arkitekter
items.content_html: The project is rooted in a pedagogical and architectural vision inspired by the Lecoq School in Paris, where space and surroundings actively participate in the learning process. This philosophy shaped an architecture integrating nature, movement, and flexibility. A key expression is the main black box/white box hall, which can transform into a light-filled space through large glass façades, bringing daylight and landscape into rehearsals and performances. Conceived as a landmark for Nord University's Faculty for Teacher and Actor Education (FLU), the building also connects important campus structures, strengthening campus identity, orientation, and accessibility through new indoor connections and climate-controlled walkways.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Under the Drying Nets / Multi-Architecture
items.content_html: At the invitation of the Art at Qiaoshan – Art Field Nanhai， Multi-Architecture designed an installation for the "Yugengyueyun Section--Fishing and Farming Cabanas 2.0" zone. Nanhai has long been renowned for its "mulberry-dike-fish-pond" system—a cyclical mode of production and living where mulberry trees are grown and silkworms raised on the dikes, while fish are cultivated in the ponds, with land and water mutually nourishing one another. In this setting, fishing nets serve not only as tools for the catch but also as familiar, natural elements of daily labor when hung out to dry.

items.title: [ArchDaily] "Beauty in Itself Is Dangerous:" Xu Tiantian on Moving Beyond Starchitecture in Louisiana Channel Interview
items.content_html: Xu Tiantian is the founding principal of DnA_Design and Architecture, an interdisciplinary practice that addresses both the physical and social dimensions of the contemporary living environment, across scales. Born in 1975 in Fujian, China, she received a Master of Architecture in Urban Design from the Harvard Graduate School of Design and a bachelor's degree in architecture from Tsinghua University in Beijing. Her recent work focuses on rural revitalization through a strategy she describes as "architectural acupuncture," understood as small-scale, site-specific interventions designed to activate local culture, agriculture, and tourism. These interventions, primarily concentrated in China's rural regions, have been recognized by UN-Habitat as a global model for urban–rural integration. In this interview with Louisiana Channel, she reflects on the role of the architect, questions architecture itself and the concept of beauty, explains her working methodology, and emphasizes the spatial dimension of nature.
